blocks.content: Whenever one part of a system needs data that lives somewhere else, there are exactly two ways that data can move: the source can send it over as soon as it has something new, or the destination can reach out and ask for it. Those two directions, push and pull, show up at nearly every layer of a distributed system, from message queues to metrics collection to how a CDN gets its content, and picking the wrong one for a given situation causes real, recurring operational pain.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286235081-28254401.png
blocks.alt: Push has the producer send data to the consumer proactively; pull has the consumer ask the producer for it on its own schedule

blocks.content: 1. What Push Means

In a push model, the producer of data takes the initiative: the moment it has something new, it sends it directly to whichever consumers are registered to receive it, without waiting to be asked. The consumer role is passive, simply reacting whenever something arrives.

This tends to minimize latency, since data moves the instant it exists rather than waiting for a consumer to check in, which is exactly why it is the natural choice whenever freshness matters a great deal, a payment confirmation or a chat message being good examples.

Push also implies the producer has to maintain a registry of interested consumers somewhere, whether that is a list of webhook URLs, a set of open connections, or a pub or sub subscription list, and keeping that registry accurate, removing consumers that unsubscribe or disappear, is itself an ongoing piece of bookkeeping the pull model never needs.

Publish and subscribe systems are the general pattern behind most push designs: a producer publishes an event once to a named channel or topic, and every subscriber currently listening receives a copy, without the producer needing to know exactly who those subscribers are individually.
2. What Pull Means

In a pull model, the consumer takes the initiative: it reaches out to the producer on its own schedule and asks whether there is anything new. The producer role is passive here, simply answering whatever it is asked, with no responsibility for tracking who wants its data or reaching out to them.

This tends to be simpler to build and operate, since the producer does not need to track a list of interested consumers or handle the failure modes of actively delivering to each one, and the consumer naturally controls its own pace, asking for more only when it is ready.

Pull also has a natural resilience property worth naming: if the consumer crashes and restarts, it simply resumes asking on its own schedule with no special recovery needed, whereas a push producer that was mid-delivery to a consumer that then crashed has to decide what to do with a delivery attempt that never completed.

A well designed pull interface also lets the consumer ask for exactly what it needs, from a specific point onward for example, rather than being handed whatever the producer decides to send, which gives pull a natural advantage whenever precise control over what gets delivered matters more than raw speed.
3. Push: Low Latency, Real Coordination Cost
blocks.text: 3. Push: Low Latency, Real Coordination Cost

blocks.content: The producer in a push system takes on real responsibility: it has to know who its consumers are, handle a consumer that is temporarily unreachable, and decide what happens if delivery fails, retry, drop, or queue for later. This is meaningfully more bookkeeping than simply answering whatever question a puller happens to ask.

It also creates a coupling risk: a slow or failing consumer can become the producer problem, since the producer is the one actively trying to deliver to it, whereas in a pull model a slow consumer is simply slow to ask, with no effect on the producer at all.

This is a large part of why webhooks in particular are usually offered as an addition alongside a polling API rather than a full replacement for it. Providing both lets an integrator start simply with polling and move to a webhook later once their own infrastructure is ready to receive one, rather than forcing the harder option on every integrator from day one.
3.1 Delivery Retries With Backoff

Since a push producer takes on responsibility for actually getting data to each consumer, it needs a real plan for what happens when a delivery attempt fails, a consumer temporarily down, a network blip, a slow response. The standard answer is retrying with exponentially increasing delay between attempts, giving a struggling consumer room to recover rather than hammering it repeatedly at the same rate that already failed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396030197-22836274.png
blocks.alt: A failed push delivery is retried with growing delay between attempts rather than immediately and repeatedly

blocks.title: Eventually a producer has to give up
blocks.content: After a bounded number of attempts, most systems stop retrying and move the failed delivery to a dead letter queue or an error log for manual follow-up, rather than retrying forever and quietly accumulating an ever-growing backlog of undeliverable events.

Capping the maximum delay, rather than letting it grow without bound, matters too. Doubling forever eventually reaches delays measured in hours, which is rarely useful, so most real implementations cap the backoff at some reasonable ceiling, a minute or a few minutes, and keep retrying at that capped interval rather than growing indefinitely.

Adding a small amount of random jitter to each retry delay, rather than a perfectly fixed schedule, also matters at scale: if many failed deliveries all started failing at the same moment, say during a brief consumer outage, perfectly synchronized retries would all arrive back at once and could overwhelm the consumer right as it recovers, which jitter spreads out into a smoother, more manageable trickle instead.
4. Pull: Simplicity And Consumer-Controlled Pace

A pull-based consumer decides entirely for itself when it is ready for more data, which naturally protects it from being overwhelmed. If it is busy processing the last batch, it simply does not ask for the next one yet, and nothing on the producer side needs to know or care that this is happening.

The trade is latency and wasted effort: data is only as fresh as the last time the consumer happened to check, and checking too often wastes effort on a negative answer the same way short polling does, covered in the long polling versus WebSockets topic.
4.1 A Worked Numeric Example: The Cost Of Polling
blocks.text: 4.1 A Worked Numeric Example: The Cost Of Polling

blocks.content: Say ten thousand clients each poll a status endpoint once every two seconds while waiting for a result that, on average, actually changes only once every thirty seconds. That is five thousand requests per second across the system, and only a small fraction of them ever carry new information, the overwhelming majority simply confirm nothing has changed yet.

Replacing that polling with a push notification the moment the result is ready collapses those five thousand wasted requests per second down to roughly one push per client per actual change, a few hundred per second at most. This is the same category of waste covered for short polling in the long polling versus WebSockets topic, showing up here one layer up the stack in a service-to-service integration rather than a browser-to-server connection.

This same arithmetic is worth running for any polling integration under consideration, plugging in the real expected change frequency and the proposed polling interval, since the wasted-request ratio it reveals is often far more extreme than intuition alone would suggest, and is usually the single strongest argument for pushing a team toward a webhook or push based alternative.
5. Backpressure
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286240054-354928903.png
blocks.alt: A push producer can overwhelm a slow consumer with no natural braking mechanism, while a pull consumer inherently paces itself

blocks.content: This difference in how the two models handle a fast producer paired with a slow consumer, called backpressure, is one of the most consequential practical distinctions between them. A naive push system keeps sending regardless of whether the consumer can keep up, and the consumer either buffers an ever-growing backlog or starts dropping data. A pull system avoids this by construction, since the consumer is the one deciding when to ask for more in the first place.

blocks.title: Push systems can add backpressure back in
blocks.content: Real push-based systems, like reactive streaming frameworks, add explicit backpressure signaling so a consumer can tell a producer to slow down, essentially borrowing pull semantics for exactly the moments they are needed, rather than treating push and pull as strictly incompatible.

It is worth noticing that backpressure is really the same underlying concern as the connection pool exhaustion covered in the connection pooling topic and the replica lag covered in the read replicas topic, just viewed from a different angle: something downstream that cannot keep up with something upstream, and the system needs an explicit mechanism to either slow the upstream side down or absorb the difference safely rather than silently failing.

Reactive streaming libraries formalize this borrowed pull signal as a request count, the consumer explicitly telling the producer how many more items it is ready to receive next, which lets a fundamentally push-oriented pipeline still behave safely under a slow consumer without falling back to unbounded buffering or dropping data outright.
6. Webhooks Versus Polling APIs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286242365-67401934.png
blocks.alt: A webhook lets the payment provider push the result to the merchant the moment it is ready, with no wasted status checks

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286244263-463991790.png
blocks.alt: Polling repeatedly asks for the status until it changes, working everywhere but wasting requests on a not-yet-ready answer

blocks.content: A webhook is push applied to third-party integrations: instead of a merchant repeatedly asking a payment provider whether a payment succeeded, the provider calls a URL the merchant registered the moment the result is known. Polling the status endpoint instead is pull, simpler to build since it needs no publicly reachable endpoint on the merchant side, but slower and wasteful of requests.

Real integrations frequently use both together: a webhook for fast, low-latency delivery, backed by an occasional polling check as a safety net in case a webhook delivery attempt is ever lost, silently missed, or never received in the first place.

Choosing which one to build first, when designing an API for others to integrate with, is also worth thinking through from the integrator perspective rather than only your own. Polling is always available to any integrator with no setup, while a webhook requires them to stand up and maintain a publicly reachable endpoint, which is a real barrier for a smaller or less sophisticated integrator even though it is the better experience once in place.
6.1 Webhooks Must Be Idempotent

Because a webhook can be retried, the same event can genuinely arrive at the receiving endpoint more than once, and a handler that is not built to expect this will double process it, for example crediting an account twice for what was really a single event delivered twice.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396030197-429824423.png
blocks.alt: A webhook handler checks whether it has already processed a given event id before doing the work again, making a duplicate delivery harmless

blocks.title: This is the same idempotency concept covered elsewhere
blocks.content: A webhook receiver is a concrete, extremely common real-world case of the idempotency principle covered in the stateful versus stateless architecture topic: recording which event ids have already been handled is exactly the kind of durable, shared record that makes safe retries possible.

It is also worth verifying the signature on every incoming webhook before trusting its contents, as shown in the earlier code example, since a publicly reachable webhook endpoint is otherwise an open invitation for anyone who discovers the URL to send fabricated events claiming to be the real provider.
7. Metrics Collection: Push Versus Pull

Metrics systems split cleanly along this same line. A push-based metrics pipeline has each application actively send its measurements to a central collector as they happen. A pull-based one has the monitoring system reach out and scrape each application on a fixed interval, with the application only needing to expose its current numbers whenever asked.

The pull model here has a specific, well-known advantage: the monitoring system always knows exactly how many things it expects to be able to reach, since it is the one doing the reaching, which makes detecting a completely unreachable service straightforward, an absent scrape is an obvious, unambiguous signal, whereas a push-based collector cannot as easily tell the difference between a quiet service and a dead one.

A pull based collector also has an easy way to control its own load: it simply chooses how many targets to scrape and how often, rather than being at the mercy of however fast every application decides to push metrics at it, which is a smaller version of the same consumer-controlled pacing benefit covered for pull in general earlier in this topic.
7.1 Why An Absent Scrape Is A Clean Signal
blocks.text: 7.1 Why An Absent Scrape Is A Clean Signal

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286248132-310994785.png
blocks.alt: A pull-based monitoring system notices a target is down simply because it stops responding to a scrape it expected to succeed

blocks.content: A push-based metrics pipeline has the opposite problem: if a service stops sending metrics, the collector cannot immediately tell whether that service has crashed or is simply idle with nothing to report right now, since silence looks the same either way. Pull avoids this ambiguity entirely, since the monitoring system is the one initiating contact and can distinguish a target that failed to answer from one that was never expected to send anything at all.

This is also why a pull-based monitoring system needs its own separate high availability story, since if the system doing the scraping goes down, every target briefly looks unreachable even though nothing about the targets themselves has changed, an inverted failure mode worth planning for on its own.
8. CDN Content: Push Versus Pull

A push CDN has the origin proactively upload content to edge locations ahead of time, guaranteeing it is already close to users before the first request for it ever arrives, well suited to a known, relatively small set of assets. A pull CDN instead fetches content from the origin lazily, only the first time an edge location sees a request for something it does not have cached yet, which scales far better to a huge, unpredictable catalog of content without needing to proactively distribute all of it everywhere.
8.1 A Worked Comparison

Consider a video streaming platform releasing a small number of high profile new releases each week alongside a catalog of millions of older titles. Proactively pushing the handful of new releases to every edge location ahead of the release date guarantees a smooth launch experience with no first-viewer delay, worth the upfront distribution cost for content expected to be extremely popular immediately.

Proactively pushing the entire multi-million title back catalog to every edge location everywhere would be enormously wasteful, since most titles at most locations are rarely or never requested. Pull handles that long tail efficiently instead, fetching and caching a title at a given edge location only the first time someone there actually asks for it.

blocks.title: The general pattern behind this example
blocks.content: Push suits a small, known, high value set of items where guaranteed availability ahead of demand matters. Pull suits a large, unpredictable set where most of it will never be requested from most locations, and paying to distribute all of it everywhere would be wasted effort.

The same reasoning extends past video into any large content catalog, product images, user uploaded files, software packages, wherever the total content size vastly exceeds what any single edge location could usefully hold, and pushing all of it everywhere would spend storage and bandwidth on content that particular location may never actually be asked for.
9. Message Queues: Push Versus Pull Consumers
blocks.text: 9. Message Queues: Push Versus Pull Consumers

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286252499-377774030.png
blocks.alt: A pull-based consumer repeatedly asks its message broker for the next batch of records and only commits its position once that batch is handled

blocks.content: Some message brokers push messages to consumers as soon as they arrive, while others have consumers actively pull the next batch when ready. The pull-based design gives the consumer precise control over its own throughput and makes it easy to replay or rewind by simply asking for an earlier position again, at the cost of the consumer needing an explicit polling loop rather than just reacting to whatever arrives.

A pull-based consumer also makes horizontal scaling of consumers straightforward: adding another consumer instance just means it starts pulling its own share of the work, with no change needed on the producer side at all, which mirrors the same stateless scaling ease covered in the vertical versus horizontal scaling topic, just applied to message consumption instead of web requests.
9.1 One Slow Consumer Should Not Block The Others
blocks.text: 9.1 One Slow Consumer Should Not Block The Others

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286254647-37047046.png
blocks.alt: A single slow or unreachable consumer in a push fan-out should not be allowed to hold up delivery to the healthy ones

blocks.content: This is the sharpest version of the backpressure problem for a push producer with multiple consumers: if one is slow and the producer waits for it before moving on to the next, every other consumer suffers because of the one struggling. A well-built push producer delivers to each consumer independently, so a stuck consumer only ever affects itself, queued separately for retry, without stalling delivery to everyone else.

In practice this often means giving each consumer its own queue or its own tracked delivery position, so the producer per-consumer state is genuinely independent, rather than one shared list where a stuck entry at the front blocks everything behind it.
10. Common Anti-Patterns

["Building a polling integration with an aggressively short interval when the counterpart actually supports webhooks.","Relying on a webhook alone with no polling fallback, silently losing data whenever a single delivery attempt fails.","Pushing metrics or events at a rate a slow consumer cannot keep up with, with no backpressure or buffering strategy at all.","Choosing a push-based design for an unpredictable, very large catalog of content that a pull-based, cache-on-first-request approach would serve more efficiently."]
items: Building a polling integration with an aggressively short interval when the counterpart actually supports webhooks.
Relying on a webhook alone with no polling fallback, silently losing data whenever a single delivery attempt fails.
Pushing metrics or events at a rate a slow consumer cannot keep up with, with no backpressure or buffering strategy at all.
Choosing a push-based design for an unpredictable, very large catalog of content that a pull-based, cache-on-first-request approach would serve more efficiently.

blocks.content: A quieter version of the first anti-pattern is worth calling out separately: even after adopting webhooks, forgetting to expose any polling fallback at all removes the safety net entirely, so the one time a webhook delivery is genuinely lost, there is no way to recover the missed event short of the provider offering a manual resend.

Reviewing an integration or architecture diagram with this framing in mind, labeling each arrow explicitly as push or pull, is a quick and effective way to spot which parts of a system carry backpressure risk and which parts are naturally self-pacing, well before either becomes a production incident.
11. Real-World Examples

It is worth noticing that the pull row for message brokers and the pull row for monitoring share the same underlying motivation, precise consumer control over pace and position, even though one is about processing messages and the other is about collecting numbers, which is a useful pattern to recognize rather than treating each example as an unrelated special case.
12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: This distinction is a reliable way to add depth to almost any design involving asynchronous communication between services. Naming which side, producer or consumer, should hold the initiative, and why, based on backpressure risk, latency needs, and how many consumers exist, shows real judgment rather than defaulting to whichever pattern is more familiar.

It is also worth being ready to mention hybrids, a webhook backed by a polling fallback, or a push-based alert paired with a pull-based dashboard for detail, since most mature real-world systems use both models together rather than picking one exclusively for everything.
Push says here is your data the moment I have it. Pull says I will let you know when I am ready for it. Neither is universally right.
12.1 A Common Follow-Up Question

A frequent follow-up asks how you would design a notification system that needs to reach millions of devices, deliberately without saying whether it should be push or pull. A grounded answer recognizes this is push by necessity, since a device cannot practically poll a server every few seconds without draining its battery, and then goes on to describe how the push side handles a device that is temporarily offline, typically queuing the notification for delivery once the device reconnects, rather than assuming push always means immediate.

blocks.title: Why this resonates with interviewers
blocks.content: Recognizing that offline devices break the assumption that push is always instantaneous, and describing a concrete queuing fallback for that case, shows the same operational depth valued throughout every topic in this section.

A quick way to decide between the two for a new integration is asking two questions: how much does latency actually matter here, and how many consumers, potentially unreliable ones, need to receive this data. Push wins when the first answer is a lot and the second is a small, manageable number. Pull wins when either answer points the other way.

A second common follow-up asks whether pull can ever feel real time to a user despite its inherent latency. Short polling intervals can get close enough for many purposes, but the honest answer is that anything genuinely latency sensitive is better served by push, or by one of the persistent-connection approaches covered in the long polling versus WebSockets topic, rather than trying to shrink a polling interval indefinitely to compensate.
Key Takeaways

["Push has the producer send data proactively, minimizing latency but adding coordination and backpressure responsibility to the producer.","Pull has the consumer request data on its own schedule, naturally pacing itself but adding latency and potential wasted checks.","Backpressure, what happens when a producer is faster than a consumer can keep up with, is the sharpest practical difference between the two.","Webhooks, metrics scraping, CDN caching, and message queue consumption are all real, recurring instances of this same underlying choice.","Many production systems combine both, using push for speed and pull as a reliable fallback or for consumer-controlled pacing."]
items: Push has the producer send data proactively, minimizing latency but adding coordination and backpressure responsibility to the producer.
Pull has the consumer request data on its own schedule, naturally pacing itself but adding latency and potential wasted checks.
Backpressure, what happens when a producer is faster than a consumer can keep up with, is the sharpest practical difference between the two.
Webhooks, metrics scraping, CDN caching, and message queue consumption are all real, recurring instances of this same underlying choice.
Many production systems combine both, using push for speed and pull as a reliable fallback or for consumer-controlled pacing.
